newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr puts brave face on rate risk.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr puts brave face on rate risk.

text.p: The Australian dollar slipped 1/4 cent Thursday as weak wages data added further weight to calls for a rate cut, although so protracted has this process been that the currency was fast becoming inured to the pressure.
The wage restraint, coming hot on the heels of the sharp slowdown in Q3 consumer price inflation, made a pre-Christmas cut by the Reserve Bank look all but wrapped up, analysts said.
"We think there is a strong chance -- 70-75 percent -- of a 50 basis point cut in interest rates in November," said Peter Munckton, a senior economist at Bankers Trust Australia.
By 4.30 pm (0630 GMT) the local dollar had sagged to US$0.7915/20 from US$0.7933/38 just before the data flashed on dealing screens and US$0.7951/56 late here Wednesday.
It also softened to 89.25/35 yen from 89.60/70 yesterday, but was cushioned by the strength of US$/yen. In trade weighted terms the dollar drifted to 58.6 from 58.8.

Traders said the currency had found good offshore and exporter support at US$0.7910 and this looked like being the pivotal level for the currency short term. A break lower was expected to see the October low of US$0.7850 tested, while the longer it held intact the more likely a rally to US$0.7965 was.

Traders said selling had been relatively light so far since a 0.5 point cut in the official 7.0 percent cash rate had been discounted by the markets for more than a month and the soft wages data merely confirmed those suspicions.
Average weekly ordinary time earings (AWOTE) for adults in full time work rose 0.7 percent in the third quarter taking annual growth to 3.5 percent from 3.9 percent in Q2.
That was a two year low for wages growth and comfortably below the median forecast of 1.0 and 3.7 percent respectively.
It followed consumer price data Wednesday which showed inflation also slumped to a two-year low in the third quarter.

"Combined with the good CPI figure, it consolidates our view that inflation will be moderate for the foreseeable future," said BT's Munckton. "An interest rate cut is firmly on the cards...which is supportive for credit markets but a negative for the dollar, at least in the short term," he said.
Dollar bulls took some comfort in the belief any cut would be the last of the easing cycle.

"It puts us on line for an interest rate cut after the November 5 Reserve Bank board meeting," said Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia. "But I'm still convinced it will be a very long time before we see another move after that."

The RBA was still generally upbeat on the Australian, and world, economy for 1997 and had voiced concerns the high rate of some recent enterprise pay agreements endangered the low inflation outlook down the track.

The latest data on enterprise deals were due in mid-November while the key figures for gauging economic growth prospects would be October unemployment data on November 7 and Q3 private sector capital spending on November 25.
Some analysts thought the RBA might wait to see how these panned out before deciding, while others felt an immediate cut was justified and would be on watch from Friday morning on.
Whatever the timiming, a cut, as long as it was the 0.5 point expected, it would still leave the local dollar with an attractive yield premium, particularly against the yen.

Indeed, in real terms a cut would simply match the 0.6 point fall in underlying inflation to 2.5 percent reported for the September quarter on Wednesday, leaving real yield differentials little changed.
Elsewhere, the local unit jumped to NZ$1.1284/07 from NZ$1.1158/72 after the RBNZ sanctioned a rate cut of their own and warned the Kiwi currency had risen too far too fast.
